findings.description: The inline policy grants full administrative control over EC2, S3, Lambda and CloudWatch ("ec2:*", "s3:*", "lambda:*", "cloudwatch:*") against "Resource": "*", violating least privilege. Anyone who obtains this user's credentials can read or destroy all S3 data, launch or terminate any instance, and modify Lambda code, which also creates privilege-escalation paths (e.g. attaching instance profiles or overwriting function code that runs with other roles).

A permanent IAM access key is provisioned for a human/service user with no pgp_key argument, so the secret access key is written in cleartext into the Terraform state file. Combined with the wildcard policy attached to this user, exposure of the state file yields near-administrative access to the account; roles with temporary credentials should be used instead.

The access key secret is exposed as a root module output without sensitive = true, so it is printed to the console and stored unmasked in plan/state artifacts and CI logs, leaking the credential for a user holding wildcard EC2/S3/Lambda permissions.

Permissions are granted through an inline policy on an IAM user rather than through a group or assumable role, and no MFA or permissions boundary constrains the user. This bypasses centralised access control and makes the single set of static credentials sufficient for broad account access.
